books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Labor contract, Records of the Field Offices for the State of Mississippi, Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands, 1865–1872 (National Archives Microfilm M1907, roll 47)

stimulus.text:
“…the Parties of the second Part are entitled to receive one half of all crops they may cultivate after a full and entire settlement of all claims the Party of the first Part may have against them arising under this Contract… they further agree that said portion of all crops … shall not be used or removed from the Plantation until all their indebtedness to the Party of the first Part is fully and satisfactorily settled.”

—Labor contract, Freedmen’s Bureau records for Mississippi (1865–1872)
stimulus.source_note: Labor contract from the Records of the Field Offices for the State of Mississippi, Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands, 1865–1872 (National Archives Microfilm M1907, roll 47), transcribed by the National Museum of African American History and Culture. Public domain (federal record). Ellipses mark omissions inside the passage; “the Party of the first Part” is the landowner and “the Parties of the second Part” are the freed workers.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: The contract also forbids the workers to remove their share of the crop from the plantation until their debts are settled. This rule most directly shows that sharecropping

rationales.A: A white farmer could sell his crop where he pleased; these workers could not move theirs.
rationales.B: A worker who cannot take his own crop off the farm cannot leave the farm. Debt became the chain: each year’s supplies were charged against the next harvest, so the family stayed put, working the same land.
rationales.C: The landowner wrote the terms, kept the accounts, and held the crop; the two sides were not equal.
rationales.D: Background: sharecropping lasted into the twentieth century, long after the Bureau closed.
rationales.general:
1. The rule is plain: no crop leaves the plantation until the debts are settled.
2. The crop is the worker’s only pay and only way to leave.
3. Holding the crop holds the worker, as surely as a locked gate.
4. Each year’s supplies added new debt, so the settlement kept slipping further away.
Remember: a chain made of debt holds as firmly as a chain made of iron, and it needs no lock.
